questions.q: What limitation do ARM/Bicep and AWS CloudFormation share, according to this lesson?
options: Each one is native to a single cloud platform — Bicep/ARM to Azure, CloudFormation to AWS — so choosing either also means choosing that cloud
Neither tool can detect configuration drift
Neither tool is officially supported by its respective cloud provider
Both tools require writing raw machine code
questions.explain: Bicep compiles to ARM, which only exists in Azure. CloudFormation only exists in AWS. Both are real, supported tools, but each locks you to one cloud.

questions.q: How does Terraform's provider model address that shared limitation?
options: Terraform talks to whichever provider plugin is loaded, with providers available for Azure, AWS, GCP, and hundreds of other platforms, all through the same CLI and language
Terraform avoids the limitation by only supporting Azure, like Bicep
Terraform requires a completely different CLI and language for every cloud it supports
Terraform has no concept of providers and only works with one platform at a time
questions.explain: The provider model is what makes Terraform cloud-agnostic — one skill set, one tool, swap the provider to target a different platform.

questions.q: Why has Terraform become the real industry standard specifically for multi-cloud and hybrid teams?
options: It removes the need to maintain two separate declarative skill sets when an organization runs more than one cloud, and those skills transfer directly between employers on different clouds
It is the only IaC tool capable of creating a virtual machine
AWS and Microsoft jointly require all customers to use it
It replaced the need for any CLI tools entirely
questions.explain: An Azure-only or AWS-only team can reasonably use the native tool, but a team spanning both avoids maintaining two tool sets by standardizing on Terraform.

questions.q: Does this lesson teach Terraform's syntax, state files, or providers in depth?
options: No — it deliberately previews why Terraform matters, leaving the actual teaching to this path's next course, Terraform & Bicep
Yes, this lesson is a full Terraform syntax reference
Yes, but only for the AWS provider
No, because Terraform is not covered anywhere in this learning path
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly scopes itself to why, not how — the Terraform & Bicep course in the Advanced Specialization stage covers the how.

questions.q: According to the lesson's outro, what does Chapter 6 of this course return to, and with which lesson?
options: Scripted operational automation, starting with Lesson 21, Automating VM Start/Stop Schedules for Cost Savings
A deep dive into Terraform state management
A second look at AWS CloudFormation stacks
A chapter on Kubernetes, skipping scripted automation entirely
questions.explain: After this IaC preview chapter, Chapter 6 ("Automating Operational Tasks") returns to imperative scripting, opening with VM start/stop scheduling for cost savings.
